newsitem.title: ITALY: Italian interest payments falling steadily - Ciampi.
newsitem.headline: Italian interest payments falling steadily - Ciampi.

text.p: Interest payments on Italy's debt mountain will fall to between 9.0-9.5 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) in 1997 from 10.5 percent last year, Treasury Minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi said on Thursday.
He told a parliamentary commission that the ratio would fall to eight percent in 1998.
In 1992 and 1993 the ratio exceeded 12 percent.
In order to meet the Maastricht goal of a three percent ratio between budget deficit and GDP this year, Italy would have to achieve a primary surplus of six percent, Ciampi said.
To hit the closely watched three percent target in 1998 Italy would only need a primary surplus of five percent thanks to the declining burden of interest payments, Ciampi said.
The treasury minister said that the three percent deficit/GDP target in 1997 was "very ambitious", but he added that this was the key year.
"We have a tough job that is worth pursuing. Any postponement would make things more difficult," Ciampi said.
Ciampi said that last April Italy failed to meet any of the goals laid out in the Maastricht Treaty for countries wishing to sign up to the planned single European currency.
-- An inflation rate less than 1.5 percentage points higher than the average rates of the three countries with the greatest price stability.
-- The lira back in the European exchange rate mechanism.
-- Long term interest rates less than two percentage points above the average rates of the three best countries.
He said Italy's drive to reach all the convergence criteria had increased its political weight within the European Union.
